explainBack.prompt: Why does Coxon say Anthropic is not cutting corners now yet still warn of catastrophe — what causal mechanism connects a currently careful company to future danger?
explainBack.response: Coxon's fear is a feedback loop: if companies use today's AI to accelerate building the next AI systems, each generation arrives faster, and competitive pressure to keep pace compresses the time available for safety research and public rulemaking. So a company that is careful today can be forced into safety-versus-speed trade-offs tomorrow — the danger comes from the race dynamics, not from present misconduct. That is why he proposes an inter-company agreement to limit recursive self-improvement rather than accusing Anthropic of current corner-cutting.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: An accurate answer must cite the acceleration loop, the competition-compresses-safety-time step, the present/future boundary from the WIRED interview, and the proposal as the remedy aimed at the loop.
explainBack.assessment: The article supports this fully: P003 gives the 'No, not yet' boundary, P008 supplies the loop mechanism and its unknowns, and P004 links the proposal to the mechanism. Explain-back passes.

incidentExplained.observation: The dated resignation, the accusation, the interview clarification and the company response form a comprehensible causal sequence.

artifactEvidence.excerpt: On September 9, Jacob Coxon said he had resigned from Anthropic after three years working on AI pretraining at Anthropic and OpenAI. He accused both companies of racing toward increasingly self-improving AI and “gambling with our lives.” The resignation and statement are verified events. The outcome he fears is a forecast.

In a direct interview, Coxon told WIRED that Anthropic takes safety more seriously than OpenAI in his experience. Asked whether Anthropic was already cutting corners, he answered, “No, not yet.” His warning is that competition could force future trade-offs between safety and speed.

Anthropic told WIRED it supports a lawful, verifiable way for the industry to pace powerful-model releases. Its current policy describes company risk reports and allows Anthropic to pause development. That framework is not independent proof that its safeguards work or an industry agreement.

termsExplainedInContext.observation: Recursive self-improvement is defined at first meaningful use, and 'personal forecast' is unpacked precisely where the 10% figure appears.

artifactEvidence.excerpt: Coxon proposed that OpenAI and Anthropic agree to limit recursive self-improvement, meaning using AI to help build the next AI systems. He named biological and cyber harm as possible risks, at a high level. The reviewed sources do not establish that either has happened.

A second Anthropic researcher, Evan Hubinger, wrote separately that he personally thinks there is a greater than 10 percent chance AI could kill everyone within the next decade. “Personally” matters. The post supplies no calculation, model or survey, so this is a personal forecast—one person’s estimate about an uncertain future, not a measured past rate. It is not a company probability or a measured fatality rate.

artifactEvidence.excerpt: When a frightening percentage appears in AI coverage, ask three connected questions: Who estimated it? What method produced it? What evidence would change it? A count of past events, a forecast from a disclosed model, a survey of experts and one person’s estimate can all use percentages, but they are different kinds of evidence.

“Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic and warned that competition could make AI development outrun safety work. He says Anthropic is not cutting corners now, and Evan Hubinger’s greater-than-10-percent figure is Hubinger’s personal forecast—not a measured rate or company estimate.”
A percentage can describe observed events or express a forecast. Ask who produced it, what method supports it and what evidence would change it before treating precision as proof.
